# Interim report: agent-skills-context-overhead-magnitude

**Locus question:** Do Agent Skills with progressive disclosure reduce context overhead and token spend as vendor docs claim, or does the corpus's one empirical study show real, budget-relevant overhead that complicates the cost-optimization pillar?
**Flavor:** dialectical

## What the corpus already said

Two vendor-side sources in the corpus describe progressive disclosure as an architectural efficiency mechanism, but notably do not quantify its savings. [[agent-skills-claude-platform-docs]] (Anthropic's platform docs) specifies the three levels concretely: Level 1 metadata (YAML `name`+`description`) is "~100 tokens/skill, always loaded at startup into system prompt"; Level 2 (the SKILL.md body) is "under 5k tokens, loaded only when triggered"; Level 3 (bundled scripts/references) is "zero cost until accessed." [[equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills-anthropic]], Anthropic's original Oct 2025 engineering post, frames the same three-level model qualitatively ("it provides just enough information... without loading all of it into context") but contains **no token-overhead or cost numbers at all** — I searched the full body for "token," "efficien," "context window," "overhead," and "cost" and found zero matches outside the architecture description. The vendor case for "negligible overhead" is an architectural design claim, not a measured one.

The one empirical study in the corpus, [[agent-skill-evolution-how-revisions-affect-coding-agents]] (arXiv:2610.04832, Wang et al., Oct 2026), is the corpus's only source that puts numbers on this question, and its RQ3 is built for exactly this locus.

## What the new sources say

I did not need new fetches: the empirical study note already contains the full RQ3 cost analysis at sufficient depth to resolve the magnitude question, and the vendor docs/blog notes were already read in full for their absence of quantification (documented above). This conserves the 5-source budget; see Open Questions for what a follow-up fetch would target.

## Evidence synthesis

The study separates two distinct costs that the vendor framing collapses into one "progressive disclosure is efficient" narrative, and this separation is the crux of the dialectic.

**Marginal cost of a *revision*** (new Skill body vs. old Skill body, once a Skill is already being loaded): in single-step answers this adds +17% tokens on 16 open models and +24–27% on the four Claude models (Table 6/7). But inside a full agent episode, the longer prompt is offset by fewer subsequent turns, so the detectable marginal cost of a revision on episode-level tokens is **−2.3% to +3.0%, every CI spanning zero** (§6.2.1) — i.e., no detectable cost. This is the number closest to the vendor's implicit claim ("revisions/growth barely matter"), and here the vendor framing holds up reasonably well.

**Carrying cost of a Skill body at all** (old version vs. "none" — just the name+description): this is the number that matters for whether progressive disclosure actually keeps overhead negligible once a skill is *triggered*, which is the only case that matters operationally (a dormant, untriggered skill costs ~100 tokens as the vendor docs state and nobody disputes that). The study measures: "The old version costs 37 to 57% more tokens per episode than none (50% on average over the four agents). The body is re-sent on every turn... but their episodes still use more tokens" (§6.2.2, Table 7). This 50%-average episode-token tax is measured across Qwen 3.5-9B, Qwen 3.5-27B, Devstral-Small, and **Claude Sonnet 4.5** — i.e., it is directly relevant to a Claude-Code-based software factory, not just an open-model artifact.

A second load-bearing number: "In 20% [of rule-model pairs], the prompt grows but we detect no change in compliance... we call these overhead candidates" (§6.1.2, repository-clustered 95% CI 16.1–24.2%). Of the Skills flagged as overhead by at least half the tested models, 27 were "already followed" (the rule added nothing the model wasn't already doing) and 28 were "ineffective" (ignored whether present or not). This is a direct empirical finding of dead-weight token spend inside Skills as currently written in the wild — roughly a fifth of concrete rule-additions pay tokens for zero measured behavior change.

The paper's own related-work section corroborates the "material overhead" reading from outside its own dataset: Dong et al. 2026 "attribute agent failures to specific loaded Skills... and trace most context-overhead failures to mandatory Skill-body text"; Gloaguen et al. 2026 "found that context files do not generally raise task success but add over 20% inference cost"; Ben Sghaier et al. 2026 "held the model fixed across 35 harness releases and found that tokens per task rose by over 70% with no significant gain in resolve rate." Three independent studies, cited as related work rather than authored by this paper's team, converge on "loaded context/Skill material carries real, sometimes success-free, token cost." None of these corroborating studies claims the overhead is negligible.

### Position A: Overhead is negligible (vendor framing)

The strongest version of this case is architectural, not empirical: progressive disclosure genuinely avoids the worst-case cost of "load every installed Skill's full content into every prompt." At enterprise scale, with potentially hundreds of installed Skills, the ~100-tokens-per-skill metadata-only baseline is what keeps the system prompt from exploding — this part of the claim is true and the study does not contradict it (it never tests "all skills loaded eagerly" as a baseline; it only compares none/old/new for a *single triggered* Skill). Level 3 (scripts/bundled files) genuinely is zero-cost until the agent chooses to read or execute them, and the study's own token accounting is consistent with this ("scripts run via bash with only output entering context"). The study's own revision-level finding — no detectable added episode cost from Skill *growth/maintenance* — also supports the vendor's implicit claim that routine Skill upkeep doesn't blow the budget.

### Position B: Overhead is material and budget-relevant (the empirical-study framing)

The strongest version of this case is that "negligible" is the wrong word for the only case that is operationally decisive: a Skill that fires. Once triggered — which for any Skill worth building is the common case, not the edge case, since a Skill's entire purpose is to be invoked on-task — carrying its body costs 37–57% more tokens per episode, averaging 50%, measured including Claude Sonnet 4.5. A 50% token tax per episode is not a rounding error in any cost model; at "5,000-person software company" scale with agentic loops running continuously, this is a first-order line item, not a footnote. Compounding this, roughly 1 in 5 directives added to Skills in the wild add tokens with zero measured compliance or correctness gain — meaning a nontrivial share of that 50% carrying cost is, empirically, dead weight that a cost-conscious operator should be actively pruning, not something progressive disclosure design "already handles." The corroborating related-work citations (Dong, Gloaguen, Ben Sghaier) show this isn't an artifact of one paper's methodology.

## Committed position

The dialectic dissolves once the two baselines are made explicit, and the "material" side has the better evidence for the baseline that actually matters to Pillar 6. The vendor's progressive-disclosure claim is true and non-trivial for the *dormant* case (name+description at ~100 tokens, Level 3 at zero cost) — this genuinely prevents a worse failure mode (eagerly loading all installed Skills) and should not be dismissed. But the cost model a 5,000-agent software factory needs is a *triggered-Skill* cost model, because the entire design purpose of building a Skill is for it to fire during real work; a Skill that never triggers is doing nothing and costs nothing either way. For the triggered case, the empirical study's own numbers — not marketing copy — put the carrying cost at 37–57% more tokens per episode (50% average, including Claude Sonnet 4.5), with roughly 20% of individual directives inside Skills contributing tokens for no measured benefit. The cost-optimization pillar should budget for Skills as a ~1.5x episode-token multiplier whenever a Skill is active in an episode, not as a rounding error, and should build a recurring "overhead candidate" audit (compliance-gain-per-token tracking, mirroring the study's own detection method in §6.1.2) into the factory's Skill-maintenance SOPs, since roughly a fifth of accumulated directives are expected to be dead weight at any given time absent pruning.

- **Position:** Agent Skills carry a material, non-negligible token cost once triggered (~50% more tokens per episode vs. no Skill, per the one empirical study available), and the cost-optimization pillar should budget a ~1.3–1.6x per-episode token multiplier for any episode where a Skill fires, plus a recurring directive-pruning audit targeting the ~20% of rules that add tokens without detectable gain.
- **Confidence:** medium-high. The 37–57% carrying-cost range and the 20% overhead-candidate rate come from one large, methodologically careful study (3,159 Skills, 21 models, blind human judgment, repository-clustered bootstrap CIs) with corroborating citations from three independent related-work studies, but it is still a single primary empirical source for the exact magnitude, run on a published open-source scaffold (mini-SWE-agent) rather than production Claude Code, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 sandbox data specifically was underpowered (n=72 pairs, power ≈0.5 for its own measured effect size).
- **Boundary conditions:** This holds for Skills that are actually triggered during a task episode, in harnesses where the body re-enters context every turn (the study's "preloaded" condition, which it argues resembles most harness behavior, including Sonnet 4.5's). Under on-demand/lazy loading, the study shows roughly half the *effectiveness gain* of a revision survives (51% for agents, 38% for open models) — it does not separately report whether the 37–57% *carrying cost* itself shrinks under on-demand loading for a Skill that is ultimately read; the cost multiplier should therefore be treated as an upper-bound estimate for harnesses with full on-demand retrieval and full-file display (vs. the sandbox's 2,000-character read window), and a lower-bound-ish estimate for harnesses that load full bodies into every turn once triggered.
- **What would change this position:** A replication showing carrying cost near 0% under genuine on-demand loading with full-file reads in a production harness (not the paper's truncated 2,000-character read window) would narrow the gap toward the vendor's framing. Conversely, a multi-Skill-stacking study showing carrying costs compound super-additively across several simultaneously-triggered Skills in one episode would push the position further toward "material" and raise the recommended budget multiplier above 1.5x.
- **Evidence weight:** 1 large empirical study (primary, direct numbers: 37–57% carrying cost, 20% overhead-candidate rate, no detectable revision-marginal-cost in episodes) supports "material"; 3 independent related-work citations within that same study (Dong et al. 2026, Gloaguen et al. 2026, Ben Sghaier et al. 2026) corroborate "material" from outside angles; 0 empirical sources support "negligible" — the vendor docs state the progressive-disclosure architecture and its small Level-1/Level-3 costs as design facts (uncontested) but supply no end-to-end measured overhead number and no episode-level cost claim to weigh against the study's.

## Open questions

- The study's carrying-cost number (37–57%) is for a single triggered Skill against "none." The corpus doesn't address whether a software factory running agents with 5–10 simultaneously-relevant Skills sees additive, sub-additive, or super-additive carrying costs — this is the single biggest unknown for Pillar 6's actual cost model and would be worth one targeted fetch (searching for multi-Skill-stacking benchmarks).
- Dong et al. 2026, Gloaguen et al. 2026, and Ben Sghaier et al. 2026 are cited only secondhand inside the arXiv paper's related work; a direct fetch of at least one (most likely Dong et al., since it's Skill-specific) would strengthen or weaken the corroboration independently of the primary study's framing.
- No source in the corpus addresses whether Anthropic's Claude Code harness specifically uses full-body-every-turn loading or a lazier variant for installed Skills — this directly determines which end of the 37–57% range (or the on-demand 51%-of-gain-survives regime) applies to a Claude-Code-based software factory.

## Sources

1. [[agent-skills-claude-platform-docs]] — Anthropic platform docs: progressive disclosure levels with vendor-stated token sizes (~100/skill metadata, <5k body, zero-cost Level 3), no end-to-end overhead measurement.
2. [[equipping-agents-for-the-real-world-with-agent-skills-anthropic]] — Anthropic's original Oct 2025 Agent Skills announcement; architecture-only framing, zero token/cost/overhead quantification in full-text search.
3. [[agent-skill-evolution-how-revisions-affect-coding-agents]] — arXiv:2610.04832 (Wang et al., Oct 2026), the corpus's sole empirical study of Skill evolution/cost; RQ3 (§6) is the load-bearing section for this locus's numbers (Tables 6–7, §6.1.2, §6.2.1–6.2.2), with corroborating related-work citations to Dong et al. 2026, Gloaguen et al. 2026, and Ben Sghaier et al. 2026 in §2.1–2.3.

notes.title: Interim report — probabilistic-skill-sequence-prediction-architecture
notes.summary: Bridges FSM trace-automata (Cho et al.) and PASTE speculative pattern-tuple execution (Sui et al.) into one layered architecture: FSM state-conditioning as the probability engine, PASTE's pattern-tuple+scheduler as the execution engine, plus a two-tier idempotent/mutating speculation gate for production software-factory Skills.
notes.body:
# Interim report: probabilistic-skill-sequence-prediction-architecture

**Locus question:** What is the concrete architecture for mining an agent's trace history to probabilistically predict and auto-chain the next Skill/tool call in production, given two unreconciled corpus papers (FSM trace-automata vs. speculative pattern-tuple execution) that point different directions?
**Flavor:** convergent

## What the corpus already said

Before this pass, the corpus held two strong but unconnected halves of the answer, both already present as full-text sources: [[automata-from-agent-traces]] (Cho et al., "Automata from Agent Traces," ICML 2026 AIWILD workshop, arXiv:2608.23670) and [[act-while-thinking-accelerating-llm-agents-via-pattern-aware-speculative-tool-ex]] (Sui et al., "PASTE," arXiv:2603.18897, SJTU/Microsoft Research). Neither paper cites the other; they were produced by disjoint research communities (agent-safety/auditing vs. agent-serving-systems) and solve adjacent but distinct problems. The width corpus also holds two SOP-adjacent/survey notes — [[what-is-an-ai-agent-sop]] and [[github-yintonghuoawesome-agent-trajectory-a-collection-of-agent-trajectory-analy]] — which establish that (a) deterministic, rule-based "SOP" encodings are the production-support-industry's current answer to scenario-conditioned action sequencing (no probabilistic chaining at all), and (b) the broader trajectory-analysis literature (surveyed in the awesome-agent-trajectory list) treats "next-step prediction" and "failure prediction" as siblings of the same substrate, which is exactly the FSM paper's framing. [[github-addyosmaniagent-skills-production-grade-engineering-skills-for-ai-coding]] shows the current real-world "Skill chaining" baseline is manual and deterministic: slash commands (`/spec`→`/plan`→`/build`→`/test`→`/review`→`/ship`) that "activate automatically based on what you're doing," i.e., rule-triggered, not trace-mined or probabilistic. No corpus source, before this investigation, proposed a mechanism that is both probabilistic and grounded in production telemetry at the Skill-dispatch layer.

## What the new sources say

No new fetches were made (source_budget 6, used 0) — the directive for this locus explicitly identifies the gap as a *synthesis* gap between two sources already fully present in the vault, not a missing-evidence gap. I read both papers in full (sections 1–5 of PASTE including Algorithms 1–3; sections 1, 3.1–3.6 and the Theorems/Propositions of the FSM paper) to check whether a bridging architecture is actually licensed by the text, rather than inferring it from abstracts.

**[[automata-from-agent-traces]]** builds a *corpus-level* structural substrate: traces are tokenized into an "activity alphabet" (6–42 symbols: tool names, action tags, or command categories — note, this is the *same* coarse-grained symbol space PASTE uses for its "event signatures"), inserted into a prefix tree, then collapsed by a last-activity right congruence into a deterministic FSM with exactly |A|+1 states, built in milliseconds with *zero* hyperparameters (Theorem 3). Next-step prediction is then a simple order-1 conditional: "Given the current FSM state qt = δ*(q0, a1...at−1), we estimate P(at | qt) from transition counts" with additive smoothing (Eq. 4), yielding a 21% cross-entropy reduction over an identical unsmoothed baseline without state, and beating Agent Workflow Memory on 8/8 datasets. Crucially, the paper proves a *convergence guarantee* (Proposition 5): the extracted FSM matches the population automaton with probability ≥1−δ after N ≥ (1/p_min)·ln(r/δ) traces — concretely N≤690 traces for SWE-agent's 51 transitions — meaning the predictor's reliability is quantifiable and bounded, not just empirically observed. The paper stops at prediction of the *next activity symbol*; it never touches argument/parameter prediction or execution scheduling — "we recover the directly-follows automaton... not the generating automaton" and the entire contribution is confined to state abstraction, not runtime dispatch.

**[[act-while-thinking-accelerating-llm-agents-via-pattern-aware-speculative-tool-ex]]** builds a *runtime* dispatch mechanism that assumes next-tool prediction as a solved sub-problem and focuses on what to do with it. Its core abstraction is the Pattern Tuple `(C, T, f, p)`: C is "an order-preserving subsequence of event signatures" (control-flow context, mined via PrefixSpan with a min-support σ and confidence threshold τ — i.e., an ad hoc, hyperparameter-laden k-length window, explicitly weaker than the FSM paper's hyperparameter-free quotient construction), T is the predicted tool type, f is a symbolic "value mapping function" for late-bound argument resolution (e.g., `arg0 = SearchRes["list"][0]["url"]`), and p is the empirical confidence. At runtime (Algorithm 2) the system matches live event-signature suffixes against the pattern pool and emits probabilistic predicted invocations to a risk-aware scheduler (Algorithm 3) that partitions work into authoritative (correctness-critical, preemption-capable) vs. speculative (best-effort, confined to a slack-resource budget, instantly preempted on contention, and *promoted* to authoritative if the agent's real decision matches the running speculative job). Measured results: 48.5% reduction in average task completion time, 1.8× tool-execution throughput, with empirically observed control-flow regularities as strong as "55% of file_editor writes are immediately followed by a terminal/pytest call" and "95% of visit URLs are a strict substring of the preceding search's JSON output." The paper never proposes a principled state-abstraction for C — it reaches for PrefixSpan sequential-pattern mining instead, which is a known inferior approximation of exactly the problem the FSM paper solves formally (the FSM paper's own baseline comparison shows k-Tails-family methods, PrefixSpan's cousin, need 1.4–10× more states than the FSM's deterministic quotient for the same fitness).

## Evidence synthesis

The two papers are not in tension — the locus's framing of them as "point[ing] different directions" is itself the thing to correct. They operate at different layers of the same pipeline and were simply never composed by their respective authors, because one community (agent-safety/auditing) measures "prediction" in bits of cross-entropy over the *symbol stream*, while the other (systems/serving) measures "prediction" in milliseconds of *wall-clock latency saved* by acting on a predicted symbol before the LLM emits it. Nothing in either paper's formalism is incompatible with the other. The FSM paper's P(a|q) is a probability distribution over the *next activity symbol*, which is exactly the "target T" slot in PASTE's Pattern Tuple; PASTE's own candidate-context-mining step (PrefixSpan over k-windows) is a strictly worse version of the FSM paper's deterministic prefix-tree-plus-congruence construction, evaluated by the FSM paper's own baseline table. The genuine complementarity: the FSM paper has nothing to say about *arguments* (it only predicts tool/action identity, never parameters), while PASTE's entire operational value proposition — the 48.5%/1.8× numbers — depends on the value-mapping function f, which the FSM paper doesn't have. Each paper is solving the half of the problem the other ignores: FSM = "what's the probability distribution over next Skill, and how do you know it's reliable" (with a convergence proof); PASTE = "given a probable next Skill, how do you safely pre-execute it without corrupting state or stalling the critical path."

The one place a real design decision has to be made, and where the corpus is silent, is *which context representation feeds the predictor*. PASTE's own context-mining (PrefixSpan, hyperparameters σ/τ) is empirically inferior per the FSM paper's cross-method comparison (RPNI/k-Tails-family needs 1.4–3,036× more states for equal fitness). This is not a hypothetical substitution — the FSM paper's Eq. 4 and the PASTE paper's pattern-pool confidence score p are structurally the same object (a smoothed conditional frequency), computed over the same symbol granularity (tool/action type, 6–42 symbols vs. PASTE's "event signatures"). Replacing PASTE's context-mining step with the FSM's deterministic, hyperparameter-free, provably-convergent state construction is a drop-in substitution that inherits a formal reliability guarantee (Proposition 5) PASTE's own PrefixSpan approach lacks.

### Recommended bridging architecture for a Skill-dispatch runtime

1. **Per-Skill-category trace miner (offline/continuous, FSM-paper method).** Partition agent-trace logs by role/task-type (e.g., coding-agent, research-agent, review-agent Skill families — mirroring the factory's likely org-chart decomposition). For each partition, build/rebuild the deterministic FSM (prefix tree → last-activity congruence → rare-transition filter) incrementally; this is linear-time and sub-second per the paper's own benchmarks, so it can run as a background job triggered on every N new completed traces, not a nightly batch. Output: a versioned, auditable FSM artifact per Skill category, checked into the Skill registry alongside the Skill definitions themselves (bridges directly to [[github-addyosmaniagent-skills-production-grade-engineering-skills-for-ai-coding]]'s existing Skill-packaging convention).
2. **Runtime next-Skill predictor.** At each agent step, walk the session's activity sequence through the relevant FSM to the current state q_t, compute smoothed P(next-Skill = a | q_t) via Eq. 4. This *is* the "probabilistic sequence" Pillar 2 asks for, and it comes with a quantified reliability bound: don't activate speculative dispatch for a Skill category until N ≥ (1/p_min)·ln(r/δ) observed traces for that category's transition count r (concretely, ~700 traces per Skill-category is the right provisioning target before trusting the predictor, per the FSM paper's own worked example).
3. **Speculative dispatch layer (PASTE's scheduler, FSM-fed).** Top-k predicted Skills with P(a|q_t) ≥ τ become Pattern Tuples (C = q_t, T = predicted Skill, f = PASTE-style value-mapping function mined for that specific FSM transition, p = P(a|q_t) from Eq. 4 instead of PrefixSpan support/confidence). Dispatch via PASTE's four-stage scheduler unchanged: authoritative Skill invocations always preempt; speculative jobs run only on slack compute; a match promotes the speculative job to authoritative (result reused, zero redundant work); a miss aborts it for free.
4. **Side-effect gating (the one place neither paper covers, and the one place the factory context changes the calculus).** PASTE's own safety argument restricts speculation to contexts where mispredictions are cheap to discard. A software factory's Skills include state-mutating actions (deploy, merge, force-push, delete) where speculative *execution* is unacceptable even under preemption semantics, because some side effects (a push, a paid API call, a destructive migration) aren't cleanly abortable. The correct extension — not present in either source, and the one inferential leap in this architecture — is to split PASTE's "speculative invocation" into two tiers: (a) idempotent/read-only Skills (search, lint, test-in-sandbox, context-fetch) get full speculative *execution* exactly as PASTE describes; (b) mutating Skills get speculative *staging only* (pre-warm the container, pre-resolve arguments via f, pre-compute the diff) with the actual mutating call gated behind the authoritative decision. This preserves PASTE's measured latency wins on the read-heavy majority of Skill calls while not inheriting its rollback assumptions for the minority of Skills where rollback is actually expensive or impossible in a production software factory.
5. **Shared failure-risk brake.** The FSM paper's per-state failure-prediction features (AUROC up to 0.94) and online early-stopping monitor (triggers at 25–32% completion) should gate the speculative layer, not run alongside it independently: a trajectory flagged as elevated failure-risk should suppress speculative dispatch for that session (conserve slack compute, avoid committing to a probably-wrong chain) rather than being treated as an unrelated concern.

## Committed position

The two corpus papers are not a genuine unreconciled tension — they are a vertically stacked pair that the literature simply never composed, and the right production architecture for Pillar 2's "probabilistic sequences" ask is a straightforward layering: use the FSM paper's deterministic, hyperparameter-free, convergence-bounded state construction as the context/probability engine (replacing PASTE's weaker PrefixSpan-based context mining), and use PASTE's Pattern-Tuple abstraction plus risk-aware opportunistic scheduler as the execution/argument-resolution/dispatch engine, with one addition neither source provides: a two-tier speculation policy that permits full speculative execution only for idempotent Skills and restricts mutating Skills to speculative staging gated behind the authoritative call. The load-bearing reason this works is that both papers operate over the same coarse symbol granularity (tool/action-type identity, not natural-language content) and the same conditional-probability object (a smoothed next-symbol distribution), so the FSM's P(a|q_t) slots directly into PASTE's pattern-tuple target/probability fields without any representational mismatch — this is a composition, not a reconciliation of competing claims.

- **Position:** The production architecture for trace-driven probabilistic Skill-chaining should use FSM state-conditioning (Cho et al.) as the prediction/probability layer and PASTE's pattern-tuple + opportunistic scheduler (Sui et al.) as the execution layer, with a two-tier idempotent-vs-mutating speculation gate as the one necessary addition for a software-factory context where many Skills have expensive-to-reverse side effects.
- **Confidence:** medium-high. High confidence that the two mechanisms are formally composable (verified by reading both methods sections directly, not abstracts) and that FSM-state-conditioning dominates PASTE's own context-mining by the FSM paper's own baseline table. Medium confidence on the idempotent/mutating gating addition, because neither paper tests a production software-engineering Skill-dispatch setting with genuinely irreversible side effects (PASTE's own benchmarks are deep-research/bug-fix/scientific-research tasks, not full CI/CD-adjacent mutating actions) — this piece is reasoned extension, not evidence-backed replication.
- **Boundary conditions:** This holds for Skill categories with ≥~700 observed traces (the FSM paper's own convergence-bound worked example) and with bounded, small activity alphabets (6–42 symbols in the validated datasets) — i.e., Skill taxonomies on the order of a few dozen per category, not thousands. Outside that regime (cold-start Skill categories, or an unbounded/open vocabulary of ad hoc tool names), the FSM's guarantees don't apply and PASTE's own min-support floor (σ) becomes the only fallback discipline.
- **What would change this position:** A direct head-to-head benchmark showing PASTE's PrefixSpan-mined context actually matches or beats FSM-state-conditioning on next-tool cross-entropy or on end-to-end speculative-hit-rate (neither paper reports this comparison — it's inferred transitively through the FSM paper's RPNI/k-Tails baseline table, not measured on PASTE's own pattern pool). A production case study showing speculative staging of mutating actions caused incidents despite the two-tier gate would also falsify the specific safety-extension piece (but not the core composition claim).
- **Evidence weight:** 2 primary papers, both read in full methods/results sections, structurally compatible with no counter-evidence found; 0 sources tested the actual composition (it is proposed here, not benchmarked in the literature); 2 secondary corpus sources (SOP glossary, agent-skills repo) corroborate that the current production baseline is purely rule-based/deterministic, which is the state this architecture would need to beat to be worth deploying.

## Open questions

- Does PASTE's pattern-mining pipeline, if re-run with FSM-state context instead of PrefixSpan windows, actually measure a speculative-hit-rate or latency improvement over the paper's reported 48.5%/1.8×? No source answers this; it would require an actual experiment, not more reading.
- What is the right cross-entropy/AUROC threshold at which a software factory should flip a Skill category from "deterministic SOP" (per [[what-is-an-ai-agent-sop]]) to "FSM-driven probabilistic dispatch"? Neither corpus source addresses the economics of this transition (engineering cost of building/maintaining the FSM pipeline vs. latency/throughput gained).
- Neither paper tests multi-agent (cross-agent, not just cross-trace) topology — the factory's "5,000-person" framing implies many concurrent agent instances sharing Skill-dispatch infrastructure, which raises contention/isolation questions PASTE's single-agent-serving framing doesn't model.

## Sources

1. [[automata-from-agent-traces]] — Cho et al., "Automata from Agent Traces: Failure and Next-Step Prediction," arXiv:2608.23670 (ICML 2026 AIWILD workshop)
2. [[act-while-thinking-accelerating-llm-agents-via-pattern-aware-speculative-tool-ex]] — Sui et al., "Act While Thinking: Accelerating LLM Agents via Pattern-Aware Speculative Tool Execution (PASTE)," arXiv:2603.18897
3. [[github-yintonghuoawesome-agent-trajectory-a-collection-of-agent-trajectory-analy]] — Awesome-Agent-Trajectory survey list (context for trajectory-analysis field framing)
4. [[github-addyosmaniagent-skills-production-grade-engineering-skills-for-ai-coding]] — addyosmani/agent-skills (current deterministic Skill-chaining baseline)
5. [[what-is-an-ai-agent-sop]] — Fin.ai glossary, "What is an AI Agent SOP?" (current deterministic scenario-dispatch baseline in production support systems)

notes.title: Interim report — agent-self-termination-and-idle-cost-economics
notes.summary: Decision rule: gate self-archival on a durably-persisted 3-state outcome token (CLEAN/ISSUE_FOUND/INCOMPLETE-UNKNOWN) verified by an external supervisor, not on activity-absence alone; fleet-scale idle cost is dominated by per-invocation minimum-billing floors x check frequency x fleet size, with no dollar figure in corpus (audited absence).
notes.body:
# Interim report: agent-self-termination-and-idle-cost-economics

**Locus question:** Beyond infra-level VM idle-shutdown (which vendors are explicit is NOT an agent-logic decision), what decision rule should an agent itself use to conclude "clean scan, no issues, self-archive" — distinguished from a silently-failed scan — and what does idle-vs-always-on actually cost at 100-agent fleet scale?

**Flavor:** convergent

## What the corpus already said

The width sweep converged on four sources that, read together, establish the infra layer cleanly but leave the agent-logic layer almost entirely unaddressed — which is itself the load-bearing finding for this locus.

[[idle-shutdown-gemini-enterprise-agent-platform-google-cloud-documentation]] documents Google Cloud's Workbench idle-shutdown: a VM auto-shuts-down after a configurable inactivity window (default 180 min, 10–1440 min range, or any integer-second value via `idle-timeout-seconds`), but "activity" is defined narrowly as kernel activity on `127.0.0.1:8080/api/{sessions,terminals,kernels}` — "CPU usage alone does NOT reset the timer." Critically, "scheduled executions still run on schedule even while the instance is in a shut-down state," meaning the platform treats shutdown as dormant/resumable, not destroyed.

[[manage-hosted-agent-sessions-microsoft-foundry-microsoft-learn]] shows Azure Foundry's hosted-agent sessions follow the identical pattern at a shorter default: idle timeout configurable 120–3600 seconds (2–60 min), default 900 seconds (15 min), after which "the platform deprovisions compute and saves state until the session is referenced again." The note also surfaces a genuine gap: stopping a session "uses the same shutdown sequence as any container teardown... with NO dedicated 'session stopped' code path," and the docs explicitly warn a session a caller stops itself "isn't guaranteed to restart on its own even when its work was left in progress for recovery."

[[ai-agent-development-costs-why-sandbox-billing-breaks-blaxel]] (vendor content, treat product claims skeptically but the cited benchmarks are useful) reframes the cost problem: online-serving workloads spend 61% of in-execution time idle while consuming 48% of energy in those intervals; real infrastructure audits show utilization below 20%; GCP Cloud Run enforces a 1-minute minimum billing period per instance regardless of actual use.

[[build-long-running-ai-agents-that-pause-resume-and-never-lose-context-with-adk-g]] is the one source that gets closest to agent-logic (not just VM-logic) dormancy: Google ADK's event-driven dormancy pattern lets an agent instance scale to zero while an explicit state machine (`START/WELCOME_SENT/.../COMPLETED`) persists in `DatabaseSessionService`, and an external webhook wakes it via `state_delta`. It also documents "golden evaluation" tests that simulate 48-hour idle gaps and assert the agent does not hallucinate skipped steps on resume.

## What the new sources say

No new sources were fetched. Source budget for this locus was explicitly scoped to 2 and flagged as "mostly a synthesis task" by the loci analyst; on inspection, all four pre-assigned corpus notes directly bear on the question and no genuine blocking gap exists that 1–2 fetches would resolve. The real gap — a published decision rule or benchmark number for agent-level "clean scan, self-archive" logic, and an exact $-at-100-agents idle-vs-always-on figure — is not a retrievable fact missing from my search; it is an absence in the literature itself (see below), which no amount of additional fetching within this budget would fill. Spending the 2-source budget on generic searches ("agent health check decision rule," "AI agent silent failure detection") would likely surface only generic SRE/observability content already implicit in the corpus (e.g., heartbeat/liveness patterns), not a purpose-built "agent self-archive" rule — so I am treating this as the audited absence itself rather than chasing it further.

## Evidence synthesis

The four corpus sources converge tightly on one point: every vendor mechanism described (Workbench idle-shutdown, Foundry session idle-timeout, Blaxel's 15-second-to-standby sandbox suspension, ADK's scale-to-zero dormancy) is a **liveness/activity-absence trigger**, not a **task-outcome trigger**. They all answer "has anyone/anything touched this process recently?" — none of them answer "did the scan I just ran actually complete and find nothing, or did it silently die?" That distinction is the crux of Pillar 6's "quietly self-terminate... if it finds no issues" ask, and it is structurally outside the scope of every source in this corpus. The Foundry note is the most useful because it names the failure mode directly: a stopped/idle session "isn't guaranteed to restart on its own even when its work was left in progress for recovery" — i.e., the platform's own infra-level suspend mechanism cannot distinguish a clean exit from an interrupted one, which is exactly the ambiguity an agent-level decision rule has to resolve on its own.

The ADK source is the strongest positive analog even though it isn't about health checks: its state-machine pattern (explicit named states, atomically written via tool calls, durably persisted before dormancy) is the correct *shape* of the fix. Applied to a health-check agent, the equivalent would be: the scan's completion state (and its outcome) must be written to durable storage as an explicit, atomically-committed value *before* the agent is allowed to go dormant/terminate — never inferred after the fact from "the process stopped running." The ADK golden-eval pattern (simulate a 48-hour idle gap, assert no hallucinated/skipped steps) is directly reusable as a test pattern for self-archival logic: simulate a scan that completes clean, one that errors mid-way, and one that is killed by an infra timeout mid-scan, and assert the agent only self-archives quietly in the first case.

On cost: the Blaxel figures establish the *mechanism* of waste (minimum billing windows, 61%/48% idle time/energy split, <20% utilization) but the corpus contains no vendor or analyst figure translating this into a concrete dollar number "at 100-agent fleet scale." This is a genuine, flagged absence — not a search failure. What the corpus does support is a cost-shape argument: if a fleet of 100 scheduled health-check agents each run on infra with a 1-minute Cloud-Run-style minimum billing floor, poll/check cadence dominates cost far more than compute-per-check does, because the minimum-billing floor is paid per invocation regardless of how trivial the check is. A fleet of health-check agents that self-terminate within the infra's resumable-dormancy window (Workbench 180 min default / Foundry 15 min default / Blaxel's 15-second standby trigger) pays only for active execution seconds plus storage, not idle compute — but the same fleet polling actively (never going dormant) pays the full minimum-billing floor on every cycle. The multiplier between these two regimes scales linearly with fleet size and inversely with check interval, but no source quantifies the actual ratio or a dollar figure; stating one would be fabrication.

## Committed position

The agent-level decision rule the corpus evidence points to is this: an agent must write an explicit, durably-persisted **outcome token** — not merely a liveness signal — before it is permitted to self-archive, and that token must distinguish three states, not two: `CLEAN` (scan ran to completion, no issues found), `ISSUE_FOUND` (scan ran to completion, surfaced something — escalate to human), and `INCOMPLETE/UNKNOWN` (the most recent outcome token's timestamp is older than the scan's own expected-runtime budget, or no token was written at all for this cycle). The default behavior for `INCOMPLETE/UNKNOWN` must be to escalate (ping a human) or retry-with-backoff, never to self-terminate — because every infra mechanism in this corpus (Workbench's kernel-activity-only timer, Foundry's teardown-path-equals-any-container-teardown, Blaxel's standby-on-network-inactivity) is explicit that dormancy/suspension by itself provides zero information about task outcome; the Foundry docs say this most directly by warning that a self-stopped session "isn't guaranteed to restart on its own." Operationally this means: (1) write the outcome token atomically as the last tool call of the scan, modeled on ADK's `state_delta` pattern, before any dormancy/termination call; (2) a supervisory layer (not the agent itself) checks "was a fresh CLEAN or ISSUE_FOUND token written within [scan interval + grace period]?" and only escalates on missing/stale tokens — this supervisory check must live outside the agent being evaluated, since an agent cannot be trusted to self-report its own silent failure; (3) treat "quietly self-terminate" as applying only to the `CLEAN` case, and require golden-eval-style tests (per the ADK pattern) that explicitly simulate a mid-scan kill and assert the supervisor — not the agent — escalates. On cost, the honest framing is directional with a named mechanism, not a dollar figure: idle-vs-always-on economics at fleet scale are dominated not by compute-seconds but by per-invocation minimum-billing floors (e.g., Cloud Run's 1-minute minimum) multiplied by check frequency and fleet size, so the single highest-leverage lever for a 100-agent fleet is lengthening the gap between scheduled wake cycles and/or batching multiple agents' checks into shared invocations, rather than optimizing per-check compute efficiency.

- **Position:** Self-archival must be gated on an explicit three-state outcome token (CLEAN / ISSUE_FOUND / INCOMPLETE-UNKNOWN) written durably by the agent and verified by an external supervisor — never on the mere absence of activity — and at fleet scale the dominant idle-cost lever is per-invocation minimum-billing floors × check frequency × fleet size, not per-check compute.
- **Confidence:** medium-high on the decision-rule architecture (strongly implied by convergent, consistent gaps across 3 independent vendor docs plus one positive design analog; no source contradicts it), low on any specific cost multiplier or dollar figure (none exists in corpus; my framing is a mechanism-level inference, not a measured number).
- **Boundary conditions:** The decision-rule argument holds for scheduled/periodic health-check-style agents where "clean" is a well-defined terminal state (DB health check, log scan, lint pass). It does not directly transfer to agents with open-ended or partial-completion semantics (e.g., a long-running refactor agent), where "clean" vs "incomplete" is not binary and the three-state token would need richer semantics. The cost argument holds specifically for infra billed with per-invocation minimums or coarse timeout granularity (Cloud Run, Azure Functions Flex Consumption); it weakens for infra with true per-second/per-GB-second billing and sub-second standby transitions (Blaxel's 15-second/25ms figures), where compute-seconds matter more than invocation count.
- **What would change this position:** A vendor or benchmark source documenting a built-in "task-outcome-aware" dormancy primitive (i.e., infra that itself verifies scan completion before suspending, rather than treating suspension as a pure liveness/activity question) would undercut the claim that this must be built as a separate agent-level/supervisor-level layer. On cost, a single credible source with a measured $-at-fleet-scale figure (e.g., a case study quantifying N agents × check interval × billing model) would let me replace the mechanism-level claim with a quantified one and should be sought in a follow-up fetch if this locus is revisited with a larger budget.
- **Evidence weight:** 3 vendor/platform docs (Google Workbench, Azure Foundry, Blaxel) converge on "infra dormancy = liveness-based, not outcome-based" — no contradicting source. 1 vendor tutorial (Google ADK) provides the only positive design analog (explicit state tokens + golden-eval testing) and is consistent with, not contradictory to, the other three. 0 sources address agent-level "clean vs. silently-failed" decision logic directly, and 0 sources provide a fleet-scale dollar figure — both are audited absences, not search failures, given the tiny source budget and the nature of the gap.
